title: Nareśvaraparīkṣā
summary: Sadyojyoti's 'Examination of the Soul (nara) and the Lord (īśvara)': argues against Buddhists, Cārvākas, Mīmāṃsakas and others that a permanent, conscious soul exists distinct from body, senses and mind, that souls are many, and that an omniscient Lord distinct from souls exists and governs the unconscious māyā and karma.

attribution.tradition: Sadyojyoti (also called Kheṭapāla/Kheṭakanandana in some sources — low confidence)

structure.description: three chapters (prakaraṇas) of kārikās — chapter count low confidence

editions.name: ed. Madhusudan Kaul Shastri with Rāmakaṇṭha's Prakāśa, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies 45 (1926)

title: Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa
summary: Rāmakaṇṭha's commentary on Sadyojyoti's Nareśvaraparīkṣā, extending its arguments for the soul and the Lord against the Buddhist logicians.

title: Mokṣakārikā
summary: Sadyojyoti's verses on liberation: the soul is by nature a knower and agent whose powers are covered by beginningless mala; Śiva's power, acting through initiation, removes the mala at the right time, and the released soul manifests omniscience and omnipotence equal to Śiva's (śivatva) while remaining a distinct soul.

title: Mokṣakārikāvṛtti
summary: Rāmakaṇṭha's commentary on the Mokṣakārikā.

title: Paramokṣanirāsakārikā
summary: Sadyojyoti's 'Verses refuting the liberations of others': states and refutes some twenty conceptions of liberation held by other schools (among them Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist, Pāñcarātra, Vedāntic, Pāśupata and other Śaiva views) and upholds the Siddhānta view that liberation is the manifestation of the soul's own Śiva-nature once mala is removed.
notes: The number of views refuted (about twenty) and the exact list are given at moderate/low confidence.

title: Paramokṣanirāsakārikāvṛtti
summary: Rāmakaṇṭha's commentary on the Paramokṣanirāsakārikā, an enquiry into the nature of liberation in which each rival view is set out and answered.

editions.name: An Enquiry into the Nature of Liberation, ed. and tr. A. Watson, D. Goodall and S. L. P. Anjaneya Sarma (IFP/EFEO, 2013)

title: Tattvasaṅgraha (of Sadyojyoti)
summary: Sadyojyoti's short verse summary of the principles (tattvas) from māyā down to earth and the pure principles above, in the Siddhānta ordering.
notes: Not to be confused with Śāntarakṣita's Buddhist Tattvasaṅgraha. Aghoraśiva's commentary is in the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa edition.

title: Tattvatrayanirṇaya
summary: Sadyojyoti's 'Ascertainment of the three realities' — a short treatise on the three fundamental categories of the system (commonly taken as the Lord, souls and bonds; the exact triad is given at low confidence), with Aghoraśiva's commentary.

title: Bhogakārikā
summary: Sadyojyoti's verses on experience (bhoga): how the soul, equipped by māyā with kalā and the other instruments and driven by karma, comes to experience objects, and why experience is needed to ripen the bonds.

title: Nādakārikā
summary: A short verse treatise on nāda (sound) and the nature of mantras and speech in the Siddhānta, attributed to Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, with Aghoraśiva's commentary.

attribution.scholarly: usually taken as Rāmakaṇṭha II; low confidence

title: Ratnatraya (of Śrīkaṇṭha)
summary: Śrīkaṇṭha's verse treatise on the 'three jewels' — Śiva (the agent), his Śakti (the instrument) and bindu (the pure material cause of the pure universe and of sound) — with Aghoraśiva's commentary Ratnatrayollekhinī.
notes: The author is not the Śrīkaṇṭha of the Śrīkaṇṭhabhāṣya (tch:srikantha).

title: Tattvaprakāśa (of Bhoja)
summary: King Bhoja of Dhārā's concise verse manual of Siddhānta doctrine: Śiva as the one pervasive mass of consciousness who favours all; the three categories pati, paśu and pāśa; the classes of souls; the malas; the tattvas from the pure principles to earth; and liberation. Commented on by Aghoraśiva and by Śrīkumāra (Tātparyadīpikā).

scholarly.text: first half of the 11th c. (Bhoja r. c. 1011–1055)

structure.description: five short chapters (prakaraṇas) of āryā verses — chapter count moderate confidence

title: Aṣṭaprakaraṇa
summary: The 'eight treatises' — the canon of short doctrinal works of the Siddhānta: Bhoja's Tattvaprakāśa; Sadyojyoti's Tattvasaṅgraha, Tattvatrayanirṇaya, Bhogakārikā, Mokṣakārikā and Paramokṣanirāsakārikā; Śrīkaṇṭha's Ratnatraya; and the Nādakārikā attributed to Rāmakaṇṭha. Aghoraśiva commented on six (all but the Mokṣakārikā and Paramokṣanirāsakārikā, which carry Rāmakaṇṭha's commentaries).

scholarly.text: collection of works of c. 700–1050; commentaries 10th–12th c.

notes: Correction to the unit brief: 'Aghoraśiva (Aṣṭaprakaraṇa commentaries)' — he commented on six of the eight, not all.

title: Tātparyadīpikā (of Śrīkumāra)
summary: Śrīkumāra's commentary on Bhoja's Tattvaprakāśa, reading it (unusually) in a more non-dualist direction (low confidence).

title: Mahotsavavidhi (of Aghoraśiva)
summary: Aghoraśiva's prescriptions for the great temple festival (mahotsava) of Śiva: flag-hoisting, processions, daily offerings and the closing bath, treated as a public enactment of Śiva's grace.

editions.name: R. H. Davis, A Priest's Guide for the Great Festival: Aghoraśiva's Mahotsavavidhi (OUP, 2010)

title: Pañcāvaraṇastava
summary: Aghoraśiva's hymn describing, for visualization, Sadāśiva and the five enclosures (āvaraṇa) of his retinue.

editions.name: ed. D. Goodall et al., The Pañcāvaraṇastava of Aghoraśivācārya (IFP/EFEO, 2005)

title: Prāyaścittasamuccaya (of Trilocanaśiva)
summary: Trilocanaśiva's compendium of expiations (prāyaścitta) for initiated Śaivas and priests who breach their observances.

title: Śivajñānabodha (Sanskrit)
summary: Twelve Sanskrit verses (sūtras) on pati, paśu and pāśa, liberation and the conduct of the freed, which the Tamil tradition holds to be from the Raurava Āgama and to be the source that Meykaṇṭār rendered as the Civañāṉa Pōtam; commented in Sanskrit by Śivāgrayogin.

attribution.tradition: a section (the pāśavimocana chapter) of the Raurava Āgama, revealed by Śiva
attribution.scholarly: not found in surviving Raurava material; whether it precedes the Tamil Civañāṉa Pōtam or is a Sanskrit rendering of it is disputed

title: Kuñcitāṅghristava
summary: Umāpati Śivācārya's Sanskrit hymn to the raised ('bent') foot of Naṭarāja at Chidambaram, the foot of grace.

title: Tirumuṟai
summary: The twelve-book canon of Tamil Śaiva sacred literature: (1–3) Tiruñāṉacampantar's hymns; (4–6) Tirunāvukkaracar's (Appar's) hymns; (7) Cuntarar's hymns — books 1–7 together are the Tēvāram; (8) Māṇikkavācakar's Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār; (9) the Tiruvicaippā of nine poets and Cēntaṉār's Tiruppallāṇṭu; (10) Tirumūlar's Tirumantiram; (11) forty works by twelve poets (Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār, Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ, Nakkīrar, Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār, Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi and others); (12) Cēkkiḻār's Periya Purāṇam.
alt_titles: the Tamil Veda (Tamiḻ maṟai) of the Śaivas

attribution.tradition: Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi, at the request of the Cōḻa king Rājarāja (Apayakulacēkaraṉ), recovered the hymns from a sealed room in the Chidambaram temple and arranged books 1–11; the Periya Purāṇam was added as the twelfth (Tirumuṟaikaṇṭa Purāṇam)
attribution.scholarly: compiled in stages c. 10th–12th c.; the identity of the king and the exact stages are debated

scholarly.text: contents c. 6th–12th c.; compilation c. 10th–12th c.

structure.description: 12 books (tirumuṟai): 1–3 Campantar (c. 384 patikams), 4–6 Appar (c. 312), 7 Cuntarar (c. 100), 8 Tiruvācakam + Tirukkōvaiyār, 9 Tiruvicaippā + Tiruppallāṇṭu, 10 Tirumantiram, 11 forty works by twelve authors, 12 Periya Purāṇam. Hymn counts as usually given (moderate).

title: Tēvāram
summary: The hymns (patikams, usually of ten or eleven verses, set to melodic modes called paṇ) of the three samayācāryas — Campantar (Tirumuṟai 1–3), Appar (4–6) and Cuntarar (7) — sung at some 274 temples of the Tamil land and beyond; praise of Śiva's forms, deeds and shrines, confession, surrender, and polemic against Jains and Buddhists. Sung daily in temples by ōtuvārs.

tradition.text: the tradition says only a fraction survived (e.g. Campantar is said to have sung 16,000 patikams — low confidence)

scholarly.text: 7th–9th c. (Appar and Campantar 7th c.; Cuntarar 8th–early 9th c.)

structure.description: about 796 patikams (Campantar c. 384, Appar c. 312, Cuntarar c. 100), c. 8,000 verses — counts as usually given

title: Tiruvācakam
summary: Māṇikkavācakar's 'Sacred Utterance': 51 poems (c. 656 verses) of longing, confession, ecstatic surrender and praise of Śiva who came to him as guru at Tirupperunturai; opens with the Civapurāṇam; includes the Tiruvempāvai and Tiruppaḷḷiyeḻucci. The tradition says Śiva himself wrote it down.

tradition.text: much of the Tamil tradition places Māṇikkavācakar before the Tēvāram poets (some traditional scholars: 3rd c. or earlier)

title: Tirukkōvaiyār
summary: Māṇikkavācakar's 400-verse love poem in the kōvai genre, set at Tillai (Chidambaram); the tradition reads the heroine's love as the soul's for Śiva. Tradition: Śiva asked for it after writing down the Tiruvācakam.

title: Tiruvicaippā
summary: Hymns of nine poets forming the ninth Tirumuṟai — Tirumāḷikaittēvar, Cēntaṉār, Karuvūrttēvar, Pūnturutti Nampi Kāṭanampi, Kaṇṭarātittar, Vēṇāṭṭaṭikaḷ, Tiruvāliyamutaṉār, Puruṭōttama Nampi and Cētirāyar — many addressed to Naṭarāja at Chidambaram and to the Rājarājeśvaram at Tañcāvūr.
notes: The nine names are given at moderate confidence; identification of Karuvūrttēvar with the Siddhar Karuvūrār is traditional.

title: Tiruppallāṇṭu
summary: Cēntaṉār's benedictory hymn ('may he live many years') to Śiva, sung at the close of temple worship; part of the ninth Tirumuṟai.

title: Tirumantiram
summary: Tirumūlar's c. 3,000 verses in nine sections (tantras) and a preface: ethics, impermanence and the guru; Śiva's greatness, his five acts and the classes of souls; eightfold yoga and its powers; mantras, cakras and the Goddess; the Śaiva schools and the four paths; the guru and grace; the centres, liṅga and the realized; the states of the soul and the tattvas; and the Dance, the five letters and the experience of Śiva. It declares 'love is Śiva' and 'one family, one God', and joins Vedānta and Siddhānta.

attribution.tradition: a siddha from Kailāsa who entered the body of the cowherd Mūlaṉ and sang one verse a year for 3,000 years
attribution.scholarly: a single or composite author; parts may be later additions

tradition.text: Tirumūlar lived through 3,000 years of yoga

scholarly.text: disputed: proposals range from c. 5th to c. 10th c.; the 7th–8th c. is often given

structure.description: preface (pāyiram) + 9 tantras, c. 3,047 verses; the tradition links the nine tantras to nine Āgamas

title: Patiṉoṉṟām Tirumuṟai (the eleventh book)
summary: Forty works by twelve poets: Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār's three poems, Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ's three, Aiyaṭikaḷ Kāṭavarkōṉ's Kṣēttirat Tiruveṇpā, Nakkīrar's Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai and other poems, Kallāṭar, Kapilar, Paraṇar, Iḷampperumāṉ Aṭikaḷ, Atiravāciyaṭikaḷ, Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār's five poems, and Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi's ten works including the Tiruttoṇṭar Tiruvantāti.
notes: Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār of this book is often distinguished by scholars from the later Siddhar Paṭṭiṉattār (tch:pattinattar, U22); the tradition often identifies them.

title: Aṟputat Tiruvantāti
summary: Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār's 'Wondrous antāti' of about 101 veṇpā verses: love for Śiva from birth, his forms and dance, and the plea never to forget him.

title: Tiruviraṭṭai Maṇimālai
summary: Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār's twenty-verse 'double gem garland' of alternating metres praising Śiva.

title: Tiruvālaṅkāṭṭu Mūtta Tiruppatikam
summary: Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār's two 'elder patikams' on Śiva dancing in the cremation ground at Tiruvālaṅkāṭu among ghouls — among the oldest Tamil patikams and the earliest Tamil descriptions of Śiva's dance.

title: Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai
summary: Nakkīrar's guide-poem directing a seeker to Murukaṉ at his six abodes; first of the Sangam Pattuppāṭṭu and included in the eleventh Tirumuṟai.

scholarly.text: c. 5th–6th c. (later than most Sangam poems)

title: Tiruttoṇṭar Tiruvantāti
summary: Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi's antāti expanding Cuntarar's list of devotees with a verse on each saint; a source of Cēkkiḻār's Periya Purāṇam.

title: Tirukkayilāya Ñāṉa Ulā
summary: Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ's ulā ('procession') poem on Śiva at Kailāsa, said to have been recited there; also called Āti Ulā, the first Tamil ulā.

title: Kṣēttirat Tiruveṇpā
summary: Aiyaṭikaḷ Kāṭavarkōṉ's veṇpās on the shrines he visited after giving up his throne, each urging the mind to seek Śiva before death.

title: Periya Purāṇam
summary: Cēkkiḻār's 'Great Purāṇa' (Tiruttoṇṭar Purāṇam): the lives of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs and the nine groups of devotees named in Cuntarar's Tiruttoṇṭattokai, framed by Cuntarar's own story; the twelfth Tirumuṟai and the charter of Tamil Śaiva sainthood.

attribution.tradition: composed by Cēkkiḻār in the thousand-pillared hall at Chidambaram, Śiva giving the opening word 'ulakelām'
attribution.scholarly: Cēkkiḻār, a minister of Kulōttuṅka II

structure.description: 13 sections (carukkams); over four thousand verses (counts of c. 4,250–4,290 are given)

title: Tirumuṟaikaṇṭa Purāṇam
summary: A short purāṇam on the recovery of the Tēvāram manuscripts at Chidambaram and their arrangement into the Tirumuṟai by Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi.

title: Kōyil Purāṇam
summary: Umāpati Civācāriyār's Tamil purāṇa of Chidambaram (Kōyil, 'the Temple'): Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda, the dance of Naṭarāja and the sanctity of Tillai.

title: Tiruttoṇṭar Purāṇa Cāram
summary: Umāpati Civācāriyār's summary in verse of the Periya Purāṇam.

title: Cēkkiḻār Purāṇam
summary: A verse life of Cēkkiḻār attributed to Umāpati Civācāriyār: his ministry under the Cōḻa king and the composition of the Periya Purāṇam.

title: Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam
summary: Parañcōti Muṉivar's purāṇam of the sixty-four 'sacred sports' of Śiva at Madurai, including the stories of Māṇikkavācakar (the foxes turned into horses, the Lord carrying earth for the Vaikai embankment) and of Campantar's contest with the Jains.
notes: An earlier Tiruvālavāyuṭaiyār Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam (Perumpaṟṟappuliyūr Nampi, c. 13th c.) is noted at low confidence.

title: Meykaṇṭa Śāstras (the fourteen)
summary: The fourteen doctrinal treatises (cittānta cāttiram) of Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta: (1) Tiruvuntiyār, (2) Tirukkaḷiṟṟuppaṭiyār, (3) Civañāṉa Pōtam, (4) Civañāṉa Cittiyār, (5) Irupā Irupatu, (6) Uṇmai Viḷakkam, (7) Civappirakācam, (8) Tiruvaruṭpayaṉ, (9) Viṉāveṇpā, (10) Poṟṟippahṟoṭai, (11) Koṭikkavi, (12) Neñcuviṭu Tūtu, (13) Uṇmai Neṟi Viḷakkam, (14) Caṅkaṟpa Nirākaraṇam.

structure.description: 14 treatises: 2 by the two Uyyavanta Tēvanāyaṉārs, 1 by Meykaṇṭār, 2 by Aruṇanti, 1 by Maṉavācakaṅkaṭantār, 8 by Umāpati (one disputed)

notes: Named after Meykaṇṭār though two precede him; the canonical order is the tradition's.

title: Tiruvuntiyār
summary: 45 short verses (with the refrain 'untīpaṟa') by Uyyavanta Tēvanāyaṉār of Tiruviyalūr on grace, the guru and the non-dual union reached by grace, the earliest of the fourteen.

title: Tirukkaḷiṟṟuppaṭiyār
summary: 100 verses by Uyyavanta Tēvanāyaṉār of Tirukkaṭavūr expounding the Tiruvuntiyār: the guru's grace, the dissolution of the ego and the state of the jīvanmukta. Tradition: placed at the foot of the elephant-flanked steps (kaḷiṟṟuppaṭi) of the Chidambaram hall, the stone elephant accepted it.

title: Civañāṉa Pōtam
summary: Meykaṇṭār's twelve sūtras (40 lines) with his own prose gloss (vārttikam) and illustrative verses: proof of the Lord from the threefold world (1), the Lord's non-dual relation to souls (2), proof of the soul (3), the soul and the inner organs (4), how souls know through the Lord (5), the Real (6), the soul as sadasat (7), the guru's grace (8), purification by the five letters (9), removal of bonds (10), union with Śiva (11), and the conduct of the freed (12). The foundational text of Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta.

attribution.tradition: Meykaṇṭār's Tamil rendering (moḻipeyarppu) of twelve Sanskrit verses of the Raurava Āgama (src:sivajnanabodha), with his own gloss
attribution.scholarly: Meykaṇṭār; whether it translates a prior Sanskrit text or the Sanskrit verses render the Tamil is disputed

structure.description: 12 sūtras in 4 sections (iyal) of three: proofs (1–3), definitions (4–6), means (7–9), fruit (10–12); sūtras 1–6 'general', 7–12 'specific'

editions.name: J. M. Nallaswami Pillai, Sivagnana Botham of Meikanda Deva (1895) — moderate confidence

title: Civañāṉa Cittiyār
summary: Aruṇanti Civācāriyār's great exposition of the Civañāṉa Pōtam in two parts: Parapakkam, stating and refuting fourteen rival schools (Lokāyata, four Buddhist schools, Jains, Ājīvikas, Mīmāṃsakas, Māyāvāda Vedānta, Pāñcarātra and others), and Cupakkam, the Siddhānta's own doctrine arranged under the twelve sūtras (God, soul, bonds, grace, the kinds of initiation, the four paths, liberation).

structure.description: Parapakkam (c. 301 verses) and Cupakkam (c. 328 verses) — counts moderate confidence

notes: Six classical commentaries are traditionally counted (incl. Civañāṉa Muṉivar's and Civākkiraiyōki's) — low confidence.

title: Irupā Irupatu
summary: Aruṇanti's twenty verses in alternating veṇpā and akaval metres, posed as a disciple's questions to his guru Meykaṇṭār on bondage, the malas and grace.

title: Uṇmai Viḷakkam
summary: Maṉavācakaṅkaṭantār's 54 verses in question-and-answer form: the 36 tattvas, the three padārthas, the five letters and their meaning, and the dance of Naṭarāja as the five acts.

title: Civappirakācam
summary: Umāpati Civācāriyār's 100-verse compendium of the whole system (the guru, the three padārthas, the malas, the avasthās, the means and liberation).

title: Tiruvaruṭpayaṉ
summary: Umāpati Civācāriyār's 'Fruit of Divine Grace': 100 couplets in the kuṟaḷ metre in ten chapters — the Lord, souls, the dark mala, grace, grace embodied as the guru, the way of knowing, the soul's enlightenment, the attainment of bliss, the five letters, and the state of the attained.

title: Viṉāveṇpā
summary: Umāpati's thirteen veṇpās put as questions (viṉā) to Meykaṇṭār on the relation of soul, mala and Śiva in union.

title: Poṟṟippahṟoṭai
summary: Umāpati's long praise-poem on Śiva's grace working through the soul's states from bondage to release.

title: Koṭikkavi
summary: Umāpati's four verses on the flag (koṭi) of Śiva; tradition: sung at Chidambaram when the festival flag would not rise, whereupon it rose.

title: Neñcuviṭu Tūtu
summary: Umāpati's 'message sent by the heart' (tūtu genre, c. 129 couplets): the soul sends its heart to Śiva, expounding the path to grace and the lineage of teachers.

title: Uṇmai Neṟi Viḷakkam
summary: Six verses setting out the ten stages (tacakāriyam): the form, seeing and purification of the tattvas, of the soul, and of Śiva, culminating in Śiva-yoga and Śiva-bhoga.

attribution.tradition: Umāpati Civācāriyār (some manuscripts and scholars: Tattuvanātar of Cīkāḻi)

title: Caṅkaṟpa Nirākaraṇam
summary: Umāpati's refutation of nine views close to the Siddhānta — Māyāvāda, Aikyavāda, Pāṣāṇavāda, Bhedavāda, Śivasamavāda, Saṅkrāntavāda, Īśvarāvikāravāda, Nimittakāraṇapariṇāmavāda and Śivādvaita — especially on the relation of the freed soul to Śiva.
notes: The list of nine is given at moderate confidence.

title: Civañāṉa Māpāṭiyam
summary: Civañāṉa Muṉivar's 'great commentary' on the Civañāṉa Pōtam, the classical scholastic exposition of Tamil Siddhānta, defending it against Advaita and against rival Śaiva readings.

title: Civañāṉa Pōtac Ciṟṟurai
summary: Civañāṉa Muṉivar's short commentary on the Civañāṉa Pōtam, the standard teaching gloss.

title: Tirukkuṟaḷ
summary: Tiruvaḷḷuvar's 1,330 couplets (kuṟaḷ-veṇpā) in 133 chapters of ten, in three books: Aṟam (virtue, 38 chapters — preface, the householder's life, the renunciant's life, fate), Poruḷ (wealth and polity, 70 chapters) and Iṉpam/Kāmam (love, 25 chapters). It names no sectarian deity; its ethics of non-killing, abstention from meat, truthfulness, love, gratitude and renunciation are claimed by Śaivas, Jains, Vaiṣṇavas, Buddhists, and as non-sectarian ('the common scripture').
alt_titles: Ulakap Potumaṟai (common scripture of the world)

attribution.tradition: Tiruvaḷḷuvar; presented at the Madurai academy (Caṅkam), where the plank accepted only it (Tiruvaḷḷuva Mālai); Jain tradition identifies the author with Elācārya/Kundakunda
attribution.scholarly: a single author, Tiruvaḷḷuvar, of unknown affiliation; possibly Jain-influenced

tradition.text: a Sangam-age work; the Tiruvaḷḷuvar era used in Tamil Nadu reckons from 31 BCE (fixed by Tamil scholars in 1921)

scholarly.text: c. 5th–6th c. CE (Zvelebil and others); proposals range from c. 300 BCE to the 6th c. CE

structure.description: 3 books (pāl), 133 chapters (atikāram) × 10 couplets = 1,330 kuṟaḷs; Aṟam 38, Poruḷ 70, Iṉpam 25 chapters

editions.name: G. U. Pope, The Sacred Kurral of Tiruvalluva-Nayanar (1886)

notes: lineages lists traditions that have claimed or canonically commented the text (Śaiva, Jain, Vaiṣṇava), not an established affiliation; the Buddhist and non-sectarian claims are in dsp:affiliation-of-tirukkural.

title: Tiruvaḷḷuva Mālai
summary: A garland of some 55 praise-verses on the Kuṟaḷ ascribed by tradition to the goddess of speech, a voice from the sky and the poets of the Madurai academy.

attribution.tradition: the Sangam poets and divine voices

title: Parimēlaḻakar's commentary on the Tirukkuṟaḷ
summary: The most influential of the ten medieval Kuṟaḷ commentaries: reads the Kuṟaḷ through dharmaśāstra and Āgamic categories (e.g. glossing 'the one of eight qualities' of Kuṟaḷ 9 with Śiva's eight attributes as listed in the Śaiva Āgamas), within the four aims of life.

title: Maṇakkuṭavar's commentary on the Tirukkuṟaḷ
summary: The oldest surviving Kuṟaḷ commentary; the commentator's own affiliation is disputed (some consider him a Jain).
